title: Adaptive KV tiling and NCCL placement — sketch
content:
Summary:
This note sketches an adaptive KV-tiling + NCCL placement approach for multi-GPU inference. Goal: reduce cross-GPU NCCL pressure and peak device memory while keeping latency SLOs for mixed sequence workloads. The key idea is to dynamically choose a KV tiling granularity (tile size in tokens/kv-rows) and map tiles to GPUs using a cost model that balances NVLink/NCCL hop counts, per-GPU free memory, and request affinity (hot prefixes).

Motivation / Observed pain points:
- Large context LLMs drive large KV working sets; naive full-KV replication or coarse sharding either wastes memory or causes frequent NCCL allgather spikes.
- Static shard assignments lead to severe tail latency when request patterns concentrate on a subset of prefixes or users.
- Existing NCCL tuning (ring vs tree) helps bandwidth but doesn't address high-frequency small transfers driven by KV misses.

Design overview (high level):
1) KV-tiling: split KV cache per layer into small tiles (configurable tile_rows). Each tile represents contiguous position ranges (e.g., 64–512 tokens).
2) Adaptive placement controller: periodically (100–1000ms) compute tile->GPU mapping using a cost model; ability to migrate tiles incrementally.
3) Hotspot replication: hot tiles (above access threshold) are opportunistically replicated to 1–2 GPUs to avoid repeated network fetches. Replication limited by memory budget.
4) NCCL-aware placement: cost model includes topology-aware communication cost (gpuA->gpuB cost via NCCL ring segments, NVLink lanes, PCIe), favoring intra-node placements that minimize multi-hop transfers.
5) Scheduling hook: request scheduler uses mapping to prefer dispatching inference subgraphs to GPUs that own needed tiles; if missing tiles are present remotely, scheduler chooses among options that minimize expected added latency (transfer + execution).

Data structures and metadata: (in-memory small tables)
- TileCatalog: tile_id -> (layer, start_pos, end_pos, size_bytes, owners=[gpus], last_access_ts, access_count)
- GPUInventory: gpu_id -> (free_mem, bandwidth_score, local_hot_count)
- TopologyGraph: pre-computed link-speed matrix between GPUs (weights for cost model)

Placement cost model (sketch):
cost(tile, gpu) = alpha * estimated_remote_bandwidth_cost(tile, gpu) + beta * memory_pressure_penalty(gpu) + gamma * load_balance_penalty(gpu) - delta * affinity_score(tile, gpu)
where estimated_remote_bandwidth_cost sums expected bytes transferred times measured link latency/bandwidth between owner(gpu_i) and candidate gpu. affinity_score is boosted where request traces show many requests originate from sessions already pinned to gpu.
Coefficients tuned via offline microbenchmarks and online feedback (SLO misses).

Migration semantics and safety:
- Incremental copy: when moving tile T from A->B, do a copy then atomically flip ownership: producers consult TileCatalog; during migration, both A and B can serve reads to avoid stalls.
- Eviction/replication policy: LRU + access-frequency thresholds; avoid replication churn by hysteresis windows.
- Fallback: if migration would cause SLO risk (detected by queueing growth), postpone or limit migrations.

NCCL tuning integration: what knobs we change and why:
- Prefer directed peer groups: when most tile transfers are between a small set of GPUs, form a tuned NCCL clique for those GPUs (lower latency than full allreduce rings).
- Use point-to-point GPU link when tile transfers are single-sender multi-receiver (replication), bypassing expensive collectives.
- Adjust NCCL algorithm per transfer size: for small tile copies prefer LL algorithms; for large bulk copies prefer ring/rma. Expose heuristics in runtime to pick on the fly.

Kernel and memory implications:
- Kernel scheduling must be aware of temporary tile ownership (cache warm-up) to avoid stalling CUDA streams. We should implement a lightweight dependency token: kernels that need remote tiles must schedule a prefetch/p2p memcpy op and record an event; inference kernel waits on that event.
- Use pinned staged buffers for cross-GPU copies to reduce CPU involvement and improve peer-to-peer throughput.
- Quantization and packing: tiled KV structures should be stored packed per tile to allow partial transfer and smaller peak memory (e.g., 8-bit packed shard for replicated hot tiles).

Scheduler integration (serving runtime):
- Request-level planner inspects TileCatalog for required tiles across layers; computes cost of executing on each candidate GPU (including fetch latencies).
- If estimated end-to-end latency using local-owned tiles < SLO threshold, pick local; else evaluate alternatives (replicate-on-demand vs remote-fetch).
- For small-batch/high-qps workloads we bias toward local, cached tiles to reduce NCCL overhead; for larger batches we accept multi-GPU cooperations.

Metrics and observability to add: (instrumentation suggestions)
- per-tile access rate and miss ratio
- tile migration count and bytes moved/s
- NCCL peer-transfer histogram (per-link)
- SLO impact of migrations (p99 latency delta per migration window)
- Memory fragmentation/usage per GPU

Experiment plan and microbenchmarks (short):
1) Controlled trace replay: run hot-spot concentrated trace vs uniform trace across replicas; measure p50/p99 and bytes moved for tile sizes [32,64,128,256,512].
2) Topology sensitivity: run on 2xA100 within same NVLink domain vs across sockets (PCIe) to quantify cost model weights.
3) NCCL strategy comparison: test directed cliques vs default ring for replication patterns.
4) Migration safety: inject background load and measure SLO violations when migration threshold lowered.

Rollout strategy:
- Phase 0: off by default, collect metrics in read-only mode (TileCatalog maintained but placement suggestions disabled).
- Phase 1: enable adaptive placement in safety mode (no replication, migrations capped, only intra-node placement).
- Phase 2: add limited replication for top-k hot tiles; enable cross-node migrations with gradual throttle.
- Phase 3: full adaptive mode with online coefficient learning.

Open questions / Risks:
- Stability of frequent migrations under bursty patterns -> need robust hysteresis and smoothing of access stats.
- Cost model complexity vs speed: controller must compute assignments in sub-second windows; brute-force assignment is too slow at scale. We need a greedy + local search approach.
- Cross-tenant interference when colocated customers have different SLOs; placement should respect tenant isolation and quotas.

Immediate TODOs:
- Prototype TileCatalog + simple greedy placer (Ethan)
- Microbench harness for tile copy perf (Li)
- Small-cluster experiments (2 nodes, 4 GPUs each) to collect topology cost baselines (Daria)
- Add Tile-level counters to existing tracing pipeline (alerts if copy rate > threshold)

Appendix: prior art and references:
- notes: relates to slice-and-stitch and per-layer sharding but focuses on smaller tile granularity and adaptive replication instead of static sharding.
- Related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serve-runtime/pull/612 (placement helpers)

Notes to reviewers: looking for feedback on (a) reasonable tile sizes for modern 70B-parameter Llama-like models, (b) safe migration heuristics, (c) whether to prefer replication or remote fetch under hybrid latency/throughput workloads.

-- end --
